Q1: Does the paper provide a measure of robustness or risk? Answer 'Quantitative measure' if the paper defines or reports a numeric quantity it explicitly uses to characterize robustness or risk (e.g., maximum suboptimality, worst-case or tail error such as 99th-percentile or maximum q-error, variance of cost, share of regressed queries). Answer 'Qualitative measure' if robustness is assessed only by description or by visual inspection of results without such a quantity. Answer 'Mentioned but not measured' if robustness is claimed or discussed but neither assessed nor quantified. Answer 'Not provided' if robustness or risk is not discussed. Plain average performance metrics (mean runtime, mean q-error, speedup) alone do not count as a robustness measure. (Short Answers: Quantitative measure, Qualitative measure, Mentioned but not measured, Not provided)
Q2: If the paper introduces a new definition of robustness, which part of the system does it apply to? Provide a concise 1-2 word categorical answer. If unclear, answer 'Unsure'. (short answers: join ordering, cardinality estimation, cost model, plan optimization, workload management, DBMS (end-to-end), ML models, No Definitions Provided, Unsure)
Q3: Does the paper include formal theoretical content: theorems, lemmas, propositions or proofs, or a formal analysis such as complexity bounds or guarantees? Answer 'Yes' if any of these appear. Mathematical formulas that only define a model, a loss function or an evaluation metric do not count on their own. (Short answers: Yes, No, Unsure)
Q4: Is there a significant experimental evaluation included in the paper, i.e., experiments whose results are reported (tables or plots of measured outcomes)? A demonstration paper that only describes demo scenarios without reported results counts as 'No'. (Short answers: Yes, No, Unsure)
Q5: What type of evaluation method is used to assess robustness? (Valid short answers: experimental evaluation, theoretical evaluation, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q6: Is robustness presented as a primary contribution or a secondary effect? (Short answers: Primary, Secondary, Not addressed, Unsure)
Q7: What method or technique does the paper itself propose to improve robustness? Name the proposed technique and, in a few words, how it achieves robustness. If the paper is an evaluation study, a survey, or a tool/demo that does not propose a new technique, or if no technique for robustness is proposed, answer 'Not provided'. Do not name techniques from related work.
Q8: Which metrics or indicators does the paper use in its evaluation to assess robustness? List only measured quantities reported in the results (e.g., maximum or 99th-percentile q-error, maximum suboptimality, share of regressed queries, runtime under memory pressure). Do not list quantities that are part of the proposed method itself (e.g., a risk score used to select plans) unless they are also reported as evaluation results, and do not list mechanisms, logs or experimental parameters. If the paper reports only average performance (e.g., mean runtime, speedup, mean q-error) and does not assess robustness, list those metrics. If there is no evaluation, say 'Not provided'.
Q9: Which benchmarks are used in the experimental evaluations? (Valid short answers: [a list of the benchmarks used], Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q10: Is the data used in the experiments real, synthetic, or both? Classify the datasets (not the query workloads): data collected from real-world sources (e.g., IMDB, Stack, Forest, DMV, OpenStreetMap) is Real; data produced by a generator or benchmark data generator (e.g., TPC-H, TPC-DS, SSB, JCC-H, DSB, randomly generated tables) is Synthetic. Answer 'Both' only if the experiments use at least one real and at least one synthetic dataset. Generated queries over real data count as Real. (Short answers: Real, Synthetic, Both, Not provided, Unsure)
Q11: Which characteristics of the data, queries or plans are deliberately controlled or varied in the experiments or in training-data generation (e.g., data skew, correlation, data size or scale factor, number of joins, predicate selectivity, query templates, workload drift)? List only such data, query or plan characteristics. Do not list hardware, software versions, model hyperparameters, training splits or method parameters. (Valid short answers: [a list of the characteristics controlled], Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q12: Does the paper include experiments explicitly designed to evaluate robustness, i.e., experiments that test behaviour under adverse or shifted conditions (e.g., injected estimation errors, skew, memory pressure, workload or data drift, unseen workloads) or that report worst-case, tail or regression behaviour as a robustness result? Ordinary performance comparisons on standard benchmarks do not count. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper reports no experiments. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q13: Does the study use machine learning in its proposed approach? (Valid short answers: Yes, No, Unsure)
Q14: What type of machine learning is used in the method? Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning. (Short answers: Supervised, Unsupervised, Semi-supervised, Reinforcement, Other, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q15: What is the machine learning category of the proposed method? Predicting a numeric quantity (cardinality, cost, latency, or the parameters of a distribution over them) counts as Regression. (Valid short answers: Regression, Classification, Learning-to-Rank, Autoregression, Clustering, Other, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q16: Does the method use deep learning models? Using a pre-trained neural model, such as an LLM or its embeddings, counts as Yes. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q17: Does the approach use transfer learning, i.e., a model pre-trained on other data or tasks that is reused, fine-tuned or adapted (including domain adaptation)? Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q18: How is training data generated in the study? If a generation method is described, summarize it. If not mentioned, say 'Not provided'. Answer Not Applicable if the paper does not use Machine Learning
Q19: How are input samples represented or encoded in the study (e.g., feature vectors, trees, graphs, Not Applicable)? If the encoding process is not discussed, say 'Not provided'. Answer Not Applicable if the paper does not use Machine Learning
Q20: Does the study handle predictive uncertainty in any way? (Short answers: Yes, No, Unsure). Answer Not Applicable if the paper does not use Machine Learning
Q21: Does the study treat generalization to out-of-distribution inputs as a robustness concern, i.e., does it discuss performance on data, queries, workloads or databases that differ from those seen in training (e.g., unseen templates, workload drift, data updates, new databases)? Answer 'No' if the paper does not discuss this; use 'Unsure' only if the paper's statements are ambiguous. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning. (Valid short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q22: Does the study evaluate generalization to out-of-distribution scenarios, i.e., does any experiment test on data, queries, workloads or databases that differ from those used for training (e.g., held-out templates, unseen databases, drifted workloads, updated data)? Answer 'No' if no such experiment is reported; use 'Unsure' only if the experimental setup is ambiguous. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q23: Which model architecture is used in the proposed method? Do not include model architectures used only as a baseline. Graph attention networks count as GNN; self-attention networks and LLMs count as Transformer (Trm); list several if the method combines them. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning. (Valid short answers: Multi-layer Perceptron (MLP), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Multi-set Convolutional Neural Network (MSCN), Tree-Convolutional Neural Network (TCNN), Tree-structured Long Short-Term Memory (Tree-LSTM), Boosted Decision Tree (BDT), Graph Neural Network (GNN), Transformer (Trm), Other, Not provided, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q24: Was improving robustness (e.g., to estimation errors, skew, worst-case or tail errors, drift or unseen workloads) a stated motivation for the design of the model or its input encoding? Answer 'Yes' if the paper states that a design choice of the model or encoding was made for such a reason, otherwise 'No'. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning. (Short answers: Yes, No, Not Applicable, Unsure)
Q25: Besides its main approach, does the paper itself use any additional, separate techniques to enhance robustness (e.g., fallback to a traditional optimizer, ensembles, uncertainty-based filtering, data augmentation, regularization against forgetting)? Do not list components of the main approach, techniques described only in related work, ablation studies, or future work. If none, say 'Not provided'. Answer 'Not Applicable' if the paper does not use machine learning.
